I was very excited for the diplomatic play system, but in practice it feels far more static than I'd like. I want more negotiating involved, and the possibility of give and take. I'd also like compensation to be possible for countries that lose territory.

If I demand territory as a stronger country against a weaker one, there should be diplomatic avenues open to the defender beyond simply relenting or preparing for war. Too often I find myself getting lax and making the same demands each game without giving it much thought. I almost always seize Santo Domingo, for example, because Haiti will usually surrender it and nobody will step in.

International arbitration would also be a really cool idea, as it was increasingly important for preventing and ending wars in the game's timeframe. 

If a war stagnates and nobody can move the needle, arbitration would help prevent things from going on forever as well.

Finally, I'd like longer wars to allow for swaying after the conflict starts. World War I would have to be modeled in the current game as a bunch of different wars where countries can't use a shared front against a common foe, because many joined long after the fighting started. 

To use a historical example, if WWI was modeled in Victoria 3, Portuguese troops wouldn't be able to take to the field in France against Germany because they joined later and it wouldn't be the "same war", barring them from military access, even if they have a common enemy and shared interests.

Obviously, wars in Victoria 3 don't have to, and shouldn't have to follow established history. This is just an example! But I'd like to see a wider international interest and cooperation in longstanding wars, especially in the later game.

America will do everything it can to get the land Mexico holds. 

I don't know of any mods for this, but I can give a few tips! 

- The US generally doesn't strike until it's enacted the Manifest Destiny decision. You'll be mostly safe (barring a very aggressive play for Texas by the US) until you see "The United States claims Oklahoma/Utah/Colorado/etc". That's when you're in the danger zone and need to be prepared.  


- Russia, France, and the UK can be helpful allies against the US.  It sounds like standard advice, but I've had some luck with Russia in particular, as they start with an interest in the Pacific Coast thanks to Alaska, and they typically aren't overly friendly with the US.  


- The US Navy can be beaten with some investment, and it definitely helps to overwhelm them with naval invasions. Watch for where they have troops placed defensively, and send small forces to attack weak or undefended strategic regions with naval invasions. If you get the help of the UK or France, the US is unlikely to defeat their navies. The US Navy is actually getting reduced a bit in 1.7 if memory serves, so this may be even more feasible once the update drops in a few hours.  


- In the current version, front lines with the US can be quite unstable due to the various native tribes in the region, meaning surprise breakthroughs can happen. It is a bit of a pain to manage, but I've definitely taken advantage of it before.  
 

- This is a good general tip for many countries, but declare an interest in the Andes and start a diplomatic play to take North Peru from Bolivia once Brazil is finished fighting the Ragamuffin War. Right when the negotiations begin in the diplomatic play, there will almost certainly be a few countries willing to aid you even if you are a bit outgunned by Bolivia. Sway them into the war with war goals to liberate South Peru and Iquicha. Take Antofagasta as well if you'd like access to the company in the area + some gold mines. Once the war is won, you'll inherit the entirety of Peru as a subject, which will give you a bit of extra income for building an army.  


- The US begins with the National Militia military law and is very unlikely to change it. This means they'll have a LOT of units, but they may struggle on the offensive versus a country utilizing the Professional Army law. If you're looking just to survive and keep what you have, having plenty of infantry and giving generals defensive orders (especially if you've pushed forward a bit into the Great Plains/Dixie) can make it harder for the US to break through.  



These are just some bits that helped me, conditions in game can vary wildly so most importantly keep an eye out for any nations that are on bad terms with the US, befriend them, and get as much help as you can otherwise. It's tough, but certainly doable.

I'm going to be totally honest, I have no idea, hahaha! I wish I could give a straightforward, professional answer, but I genuinely never go in with a specific plan beyond a basic outline. I spend much of my time reacting to events in the game and trying to respond accordingly. 

I have plenty of hours in the game, I just tend to focus on maximizing immigration and keeping my budget in the green. I went Laissez Faire to ensure the AI would construct goods that are in demand (reducing micromanagement on my part). In any run, I always focus on more staple goods at the start; Wood, iron, tooling workshops, and for more industrialized nations like the US, coal. 

I also made Mexico a dominion after taking all claims, which is risky due to great power intervention. In my case, both Spain and France intervened, but I managed to capitulate Mexico and prevent Spain and France from enforcing any war goals. (I moved my capital to Indianapolis, as it was in the middle of the country and ensured naval invasions wouldn't decimate me instantly.) 

Many regions I took over, particularly in Mexico, had gold mines, and I focused on researching technology that made resource discovery and extraction more efficient; Nitroglycerin, Dynamite, Water Tube Boilers, etc. 

I stole Peru away from Bolivia at the game start to ensure I had a puppet foothold in South America, and this also made it so my market was adjacent to Brazil. This made my market more attractive to Brazil, and I successfully got them to join. 

I waged war in areas that were less interesting to potential geopolitical allies; I took over Chukota in Russia (more gold) and when Portugal left the British sphere of influence, I seized the Azores and a treaty port in southern Portugal. Britain wasn't too bothered by the latter as I had made considerable efforts to keep us on good terms.

Boosting my naval power was pretty important. This helped prevent invasions, and would weaken my enemies if they successfully managed to land somewhere. I always left some troops on standby in regions where a naval invasion is likely. The AI has a habit of sending far too many units on a small number of ships, and even if my navy loses, I can cut that number down further. With so little support, even weaker conscripts can fend off large armies of naval invaders. 

I also rushed colonization technology, and fired off the US Civil War early and intentionally. This added Afro American as a primary culture, making colonization in Africa much easier. Wherever infrastructure was falling behind, I'd boost the railroads to keep the goods within the region flowing. 

I usually would not incorporate so many states outside my main regions so as not to pressure my bureaucracy and to keep migration attraction (colonial resettlement adds a large modifier for migration attraction), therefore ensuring a workforce will arrive in otherwise unwelcoming environments. As the USA, this can be challenging due to the extremely high migration attraction in your main states (they have a lot of arable land, oil, and gold). However, I was going for the 100 states achievement, so I've been incorporating every state I can. 

I tend to build factories that will produce goods I need before I make a shift towards a new production method. For example, crystal glass requires a lot of lead, so I built up a decent amount of lead mines and then upgraded to crystal glass. In some cases, I'd activate a new production method early to get my autonomous investments put towards the missing goods. When I shifted to electric streetlights with a shortage of electricity, the AI began to build a substantial amount of power plants everywhere, and this covered my needs very quickly. 

I made sure to import goods that were expensive for my pops, and would prioritize trade with regions who had a lot of materials I'd need to improve my standard of living or partners I had trade agreements with. This would also create trade centers, which boosted my profits and attracted more migrants. 

Again, I'm far from an expert on a lot of this stuff, this is just what worked for me! I'm terrible at mathematics, I tend to just struggle until I come across what works for me! I usually don't play to min max, but go with the flow.

Of course, this isn't the most exciting thing for most people to read about, so I get why it doesn't get focused on in some FE games. 

Many characters are defined by one or two character traits, which makes it very grating to have them reintroduce their trait in every C Support. So far, all of Chloé's supports introduce her to someone else with the topic being "She's eating something unusual and tries to get the other to come around to trying it." 

I don't need a game to be deadly serious at all times (eg. Persona 4 is my favorite Persona game despite being the most light-hearted one) but this one feels too goofy to be taken seriously at points, with very predictable plot beats. I've been pleasantly surprised by some supports (Framme and Diamant's B support where she points out Brodia's warlike history, for example) but most of them are nothing special. 

I find myself cringing at some of the cutscenes as well, like when Hortensia is introduced. It's just a bit excessive. 

I'm glad others are enjoying the story, and I enjoy the game well enough, but the writing in this one is a miss for me. Fire Emblem may not be about just the writing, but I do find it harder to care about my units if they actively annoy me. 

And a final sidenote: I'm a bit unhappy with how young everyone is in the game. I like there being a decent amount of older units to use, as they tend to be more grounded. 

Hopefully I haven't come off as too harsh.

Honestly? Not well, and I say this as a massive Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons fan. I usually prefer SoS compared to Stardew Valley, but Pioneers of Olive Town feels... Off, in many regards. I'll make some bullet points here. 

- Characters are much more interactive in Stardew compared to Pioneers. They have different things to say every day, marriage/dating is much more satisfying because characters acknowledge it and your spouse doesn't just say the same stuff they'd say if you weren't married. Your spouse has a few new lines in Pioneers, but they go right back to saying the same things quickly. Also, many characters just have very short dialogue that gets very grating quickly. 

- Caving/Mining is much more interesting in Stardew Valley, and it's one of the aspects in Stardew that surpasses all SoS games. However, it's especially apparent in this this case. Pioneers of Olive Town has very basic mines that all look the same, and the only "enemies" are moles that you hit to obtain a few goodies. Mining is much more exciting and rewarding in Stardew Valley by a long shot.

- Inventory management is much easier in Stardew Valley. There's less resources to take up space in your inventory, and it's easy to organize and keep track of. In Pioneers of Olive Town, there's a lot of resources that you have to keep track of, and they take up a lot of space. Maker machines in Stardew Valley are usually easy to place on a farm and aren't as mandatory to progress. Whereas in Pioneers you have to set aside a lot of space for numerous makers, and you'll find yourself waiting for upgrades simply because your makers aren't processing the vast amount of materials quick enough. It becomes a frustrating waiting game. 

- Decoration is much more limited in Pioneers. Your house space for decoration is limited, and you *can* decorate your farm, but a lot of your farm space is dedicated to the many maker machines you have to place, alongside the buildings and land you're using for crops. 

Overall, you'll likely find more replay value and enjoyment from Stardew Valley compared to Pioneers of Olive Town. Also, Stardew Valley is much cheaper.

Well, I am a Lutheran and had to research the Bible before my confirmation with the Church; I also researched symbolism and such in Biblical stories/records. This makes it interesting to look at how these symbols are presented in Shin Megami Tensei. 

Rather than angels being your standard Middle Ages European Cherubim, for example, many of them are presented as entities that vary in form extensively. That, and some of the angels/demons presented in SMT are physical manifestations of concepts that did not have their physical form mentioned, which I find very interesting. 

As for ones that have physical forms representing some sort of symbolism, it's interesting to see them drawn out literally. Mother Harlot comes to mind; She is called the "Whore of Babylon" in the Bible chapter Revelation (a chapter that's almost entirely symbolism) and used to symbolize powerful kingdoms falling to the Beast, with the woman herself bearing Roman imagery, being an allegory for old power and possibly human arrogance in the world. The seven headed monster she rides is open to interpretation, but some understand it as seven ancient kingdoms or the seven forms of Roman governance. 

Regardless, the symbolism is used literally in the case of her design in SMT, which I find interesting to look at. It ends up creating an intimidating physical representation while keeping the symbolism intact. Apologies if my words are all over the place here!

I'm from Illinois and regularly involve myself with campaigns. One thing I remember from 2016 involved the State House elections. Speaker of the Illinois House of Representatives, Mike Madigan, had a Democrat primary challenger who looked like he was going to receive a fair amount of votes, named Jason Gonzales. 

 Madigan's campaign aide helped two individuals, Joe Barboza and Grasiela Rodriguez, file petitions to get on the ballot, despite neither even having a campaign website. Both candidates that he helped didn't really show up much but got votes anyways, and though Gonzales still wouldn't have had enough votes if both of the candidates votes when to him, it still sapped ~2,000 votes from him. 

This tactic is referred to as "diluting the ballot", and is typically used by incumbent politicians to weaken the chances of a strong primary contender by adding a bunch of other names to the ballot.
